assessment.nobel_worthiness: Linking population-scale administrative data to intergenerational mobility created a new empirical standard. It produced geographic mobility maps, quasi-experimental neighbourhood-effect estimates and policy-relevant findings. The impact on public and labour economics and on policy debate is very large.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the clear central figure. Hendren (neighbourhood and childhood-exposure effects) and Friedman (the Opportunity Insights data work) are the most natural co-recipients. Katz, who is credited on the ballot, is more connected to the Moving to Opportunity experiment and is omitted to respect the three-person limit.
assessment.maturity: The core papers date from 2014 to 2022 and have been widely replicated or extended with other administrative datasets. Two decades of follow-up is not yet available, but the empirical foundations look solid.
uncertainties: Some findings, such as the causal interpretation of place effects and the extrapolation of exposure effects, rest on strong identifying assumptions.
The committee may judge the contribution to be primarily empirical measurement rather than conceptual.
Results on the credit for the team-based work depend on how large-team contributions are weighed.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Models of fairness and inequity aversion, together with experimental evidence on reciprocity and costly punishment, changed how economists model motivation, contracts and cooperation. The work combines theory with a large body of lab and field evidence, so it has both conceptual and empirical influence.
assessment.attribution: Fehr and Schmidt (1999) is the canonical inequity-aversion model, and Fehr's experimental programme on reciprocity is the broader anchor. Falk contributed substantial experimental and field work but is less central to the core theory, so he is not proposed.
assessment.maturity: The foundational work is 25 to 30 years old and has been tested, extended and debated for decades. Economics already recognises behavioural economics (Kahneman, Thaler), so the field's standing is established.
uncertainties: Some early lab results on punishment and inequity aversion have been questioned for generalisability and for the predictive power of specific functional forms.
The model's stability across populations and stakes is debated.
Overlap with earlier behavioural prizes might weigh against a further award in the area.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Nominal rigidities, Calvo pricing, the Taylor rule and the micro-founded New Keynesian framework are the working core of modern monetary policy analysis in academia and central banks. The practical and intellectual influence is exceptional.
assessment.attribution: The ballot credits eight people, which makes attribution difficult. Calvo (staggered pricing), Taylor (staggered contracts and the policy rule) and Woodford (the integrated framework and optimal policy) are the clearest foundational contributions. Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Gertler and Smets made major contributions on empirical estimation and DSGE implementation. Rotemberg and Clarida are not on the list.
assessment.maturity: Very mature, with decades of use. The framework survived the 2008 crisis and the post-2021 inflation episode with modifications.
uncertainties: Sharing among only three people inevitably leaves out significant contributors.
The framework's performance in the 2021 to 2023 inflation surge and its treatment of financial frictions remain debated.
Taylor's contribution is partly a policy rule, and the committee may weigh policy influence against analytical novelty.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Collateral constraints and credit cycles explain how small shocks are amplified and persist through balance sheets. This is a central mechanism for macro-financial thinking and has informed policy since 2008.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) is the key credit-cycles paper, and Gertler with Kiyotaki and others extended the framework to financial intermediation. Gilchrist's contribution is more empirical. Bernanke, who has already been recognised for the banking work, is not on the ballot.
assessment.maturity: The foundational contributions are 25 to 35 years old and have become standard in macro-finance.
uncertainties: The 2022 prize on banks and financial crises (Bernanke, Diamond, Dybvig) overlaps with this theme, which may count against it.
Gertler also appears on the New Keynesian ballot, which complicates how credit would be divided between the two themes.
How to weight the empirical versus theoretical contributions is unclear.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The China-shock work and the task-based view of technology have reshaped how economists and policymakers understand trade, automation, wages and regional labour-market adjustment. The research is of strong empirical quality and high public relevance, including for AI-related labour questions.
assessment.attribution: Autor, Dorn and Hanson are the three authors of the China shock papers. Autor also led the task-based literature with Katz and Murnane. Katz is credited but is not proposed here, because the trio is the tightest unit. The 2024 prize and the 2025 growth-and-technology prize recognised adjacent themes.
assessment.maturity: The China-shock results date from 2013 onward and have been reassessed with long-run follow-ups. The task framework is older and well established.
uncertainties: Debate continues about shift-share identification and the exact magnitudes of the trade effects.
Combining two sub-literatures (trade shocks and tasks) in one prize raises attribution questions.
Recent prizes on technology and growth may reduce the committee's appetite for the area.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Bayesian persuasion and information design provide a clean theoretical framework for studying how a sender's choice of information structure shapes decisions. It has become an important tool in applied theory, mechanism design, platform design and regulation.
assessment.attribution: Kamenica and Gentzkow (2011) is the key paper. Bergemann and Morris developed the broader information-design and robust-predictions programme. Choosing three of four involves a judgement call, with Bergemann as the nearest alternative to Morris. Gentzkow's other major contributions are in media and text-as-data.
assessment.maturity: The foundations are about 15 years old, which is relatively young for a Nobel. Adoption has been rapid and the theory is mathematically established.
uncertainties: The field has had less time to demonstrate empirical payoff and policy influence than older candidates.
Which of Bergemann, Morris and the Kamenica–Gentzkow pair should be included is a real uncertainty.
The committee may prefer to wait.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Heterogeneous-agent New Keynesian models bring household heterogeneity into monetary and fiscal transmission. They show that the marginal propensity to consume and the distribution of wealth shape aggregate responses. This changed both research and central-bank modelling.
assessment.attribution: Kaplan, Moll and Violante (2018) is the defining paper, and the trio is also well matched on the wider heterogeneous-agent agenda. Earlier foundations in incomplete-markets macroeconomics (Aiyagari, Bewley, Huggett, Krusell and Smith) are not on this ballot and could complicate the credit story.
assessment.maturity: Relatively recent, since about 2016 to 2018. The method is widely adopted, but long-run empirical validation is still accumulating.
uncertainties: It may be too early for a prize.
Credit for the underlying incomplete-markets models predates the candidates.
Empirical validation of the transmission channels is still developing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Partial identification formalises what can be credibly learned under weak assumptions. It addresses a basic problem in empirical work: the tension between credibility and the strength of conclusions. It has influenced econometric theory and practice in many fields.
assessment.attribution: Manski is the founder of the approach. Tamer (moment inequalities and set identification in games) and Molinari (inference methods and applications) are the central later developers. Other contributors, such as Chernozhukov, Hong and Tamer, Imbens and Manski, and Andrews, are not credited here.
assessment.maturity: Manski's foundations go back to the 1980s and 1990s, and the inference theory matured in the 2000s and 2010s. Empirical adoption is still narrower than for point-identified methods.
uncertainties: Practical uptake is limited relative to the theoretical importance.
The 2021 econometrics prize (Card, Angrist, Imbens) makes a further econometrics award less likely soon.
The three-person set omits other significant contributors to set inference.
